purpose: Idursulfase is used to treat Hunter syndrome, also called Mucopolysaccharidosis II (MPS II), a rare inherited disease. In this condition, the body cannot break down certain complex sugars that build up and cause harm to organs and tissues. This medication helps replace the missing enzyme so those sugars can be properly broken down.
how_it_works: People with Hunter syndrome are missing or have too little of an enzyme called iduronate-2-sulfatase, which is needed to break down certain sugar chains in the body. When these sugars build up, they damage organs, joints, and other tissues over time. Idursulfase works by replacing this missing enzyme, helping the body clear out the harmful buildup of these sugars.
common_side_effects: Common side effects include infusion reactions such as flushing, rash, hives, headache, fever, and nausea. Some patients may experience swelling, chest tightness, or changes in blood pressure during or after the IV infusion. These reactions are most likely to happen during the infusion itself.
warnings: Serious allergic reactions, including life-threatening anaphylaxis, can occur during or after the infusion, so it is always given in a medical setting where staff can respond quickly. Tell your doctor right away if you have trouble breathing, swelling of the face or throat, or feel faint. This medicine has not been shown to treat the brain-related symptoms of Hunter syndrome. Women who are pregnant or breastfeeding should talk to their doctor before using this medication.
typical_dosing: The usual dose is 0.5 mg per kilogram of body weight given as an intravenous (IV) infusion once every week. The infusion is given slowly over several hours in a clinic or infusion center, and medical staff will monitor you closely the entire time.
